scenes.audio: So Anthropic's own docs say that agent teams use approximately seven times more tokens than standard sessions when teammates are running in that plan mode. scenes.audio: So the way that I tend to think about it now is that subagents are really brilliant for looking at things broad searches, parallel investigation where not a lot of context is required, but they're actually expensive for actually doing things. Because you're having to pass that context that's then uncached in that separate window on the same model as the main window and all of that adds up over time and that's why it tends to cost you seven times as much when you're using subagents. Plus we've got built-in modes that delegate properly and efficiently like ultra code now anyway.

scenes.audio: So the current documented behavior is that if you don't set an auto compact window limit, then Claude code is going to compact when the conversation reaches the model's context limit. So it's no longer a percentage and there are per-model exceptions on top of that. So cloud sessions compact as they approach their limit and some models compact at the full boundary, let's say 200,000 tokens in the window.
scenes.label: Product Selling Points
scenes.visual: The man is speaking, gesturing with his hands. On the right side of the screen, the terminal interface shows the '/autocompact' command being used.

scenes.audio: So now what you can do is run the auto compact setting to set how full the context gets before it auto summarizes. And you can leave this automatically or you can say 50k tokens or 100k tokens and actually you set the auto compact window now to 100k tokens. Now as you go through the conversation, it's going to hit 100k tokens and start auto compacting. So instead of a percentage now, you can now set a fixed amount. And this is important because quality degrades long before that context window is full.
scenes.label: Product Selling Points
scenes.visual: The screen shows the terminal interface again. The cursor types '/autocompact 100k' and the response 'Auto-compact window set to 100k tokens!' appears. The man's hands are visible on the right side, gesturing.

scenes.audio: And while we're on context size, for number 13, historically everyone's been chasing these huge context windows, right? We were all so happy when we saw that we had models that were now able to actually take in a million tokens in that window.

scenes.visual: The man is back on screen, talking to the camera. On the left side of the screen, a red circle with the number 13 and the text 'bigger context = bad recall' appears.

scenes.audio: But Anthropic's own published benchmark from testing Opus 4.6 on a long context retrieval test where it put eight hidden things inside the context and tried to confirm if the model could find them, it found that at 256,000 tokens it could score 93%. So actually pretty remarkable it can get 93% accuracy at that high number of tokens. But then at one million tokens with the same model with the same test, it actually dropped to 76% accuracy. So suddenly you've got a three out of four chance of actually retrieving that information.

scenes.visual: The screen shows a chart with benchmarking results for Claude family models. The man's hands are visible on the right side, gesturing towards the chart. The text '78.3 (64k)' is highlighted in yellow.

scenes.audio: Which in plain English is roughly one in four of those actually failing. So one in four of your rules not actually being able to be retrieved. So a bigger context window isn't really more memory, it's basically then going to become harder to actually retrieve the right information. So I definitely recommend using things like auto compact as well.
